newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-Murdoch's Super League win a setback for Packer.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-Murdoch's Super League win a setback for Packer.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch scored a major victory on Friday over long-time rival Kerry Packer when an Australian court ruled that attempts to stop his rebel rugby league competition violated anti-monopoly laws.
The decision by a three-judge appeals panel in Australia's Federal Court freed Murdoch to launch his controversial Super League in Australia in 1997.

The decision left Packer, who had backed traditional rulers the Australian Rugby League (ARL) against Super League, facing the prospect of having to join the queue of prospective broadcasters of Murdoch's product.
The Federal Court upheld Murdoch's appeal against an earlier court ruling in favour of the ARL which banned his breakaway rugby league from kicking off in Australia before 2000.

Murdoch's son Lachlan, who is managing director of Murdoch's News Corp's Australian arm, News Ltd, told a news conference he had telephoned his father in the United States immediately after the decision was announced.
"We're rapt, we're very happy," Lachlan Murdoch said. "That was the first phone call that we made. He was rapt as well."
Rupert Murdoch said in a statement released from Los Angeles that Super League would represent a new dimension in sport.
"1997 will see the finest rugby league competition ever created," he said. "Super League retains my active and unqualified support."

The ruling leaves Murdoch free to launch his league next year. Super League, which plays an important part in Murdoch's extensive pay-television ambitions around the world, was originally scheduled to start in March this year.
While ARL chairman Ken Arthurson said the court ruling meant there would now be two rugby leagues in the country, the Super League camp did not rule out a possible compromise with the ARL.
"News Ltd and Super League remain ready at any time to discuss genuine proposals to bring both sides together," News Ltd chairman Ken Cowley told a news conference.

Cowley and Lachlan Murdoch said they were prepared to talk to any ARL contracted players or clubs who wished to join Super League, while another Super League official told reporters it was likely the competition would expand from its present 10 contracted teams to 12 in the next few years.

The most likely source of an immediate compromise between the two warring camps was over broadcasting rights of the game on terrestrial television in Australia. Lachlan Murdoch said Super League would consider bids from Australia's four free-to-air broadcasters, including Packer's Nine Network.
Lachlan Murdoch said. "A lot has been invested in Super League and it will go to the broadcaster who has the most to offer."
Cowley said he had not yet contacted the ARL or Packer, who holds television rights for the ARL's premiership until 2000.
"I haven't thought that far ahead but my memory is that they don't seem to like Super League," Cowley said.

Murdoch has invested A$270 million (US$213 million) in Super League, winning the loyalty of eight existing Australian clubs and more than 200 players. He has also signed up clubs in Britain and New Zealand with the official backing of their national ruling bodies.
Arthurson later told reporters the ARL would seek leave to appeal against Friday's decision in Australia's highest court, while ARL-loyal coach Phil Gould said the game "is in a bit of chaos".
